paras: The attempted lynching at Manly, North Carolina, was a manhunt on June 29, 1888, in which a large party of mounted white men searched for an unnamed Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, intending to lynch him. The only report found, a Raleigh telegram to the Richmond Dispatch, does not say whether the man was caught or what became of him.

According to the Raleigh correspondent, a Black man assaulted a white woman at Manly on June 28; neither is named. At daylight the next morning, "a large number of white men were mounted and in search of him, intending to lynch him." The dispatch mentions no sheriff, officers or warrant, and it ends with the search still under way.
No report of a capture, a lynching, an arrest or any official response appears in the coverage found.

The item ran in the Richmond Dispatch of June 30, 1888, as part of a special telegram from Raleigh that grouped North Carolina news under the headline "STILL PUZZLED." Under the subhead "A LYNCHING PARTY OUT," the correspondent gave the episode two sentences, placed between reports of a teachers' assembly and a child-murder trial at Keyser. The Dispatch stated the alleged assault as fact, called the accused "a negro," and reported the intent to lynch without comment.
No other paper, white or Black, was found to have carried the story.

bases: A large mounted party of white men was reported searching for a Black man accused of assault, 'intending to lynch him'; no killing is reported (A1).

The only report describes a large group of white men hunting an accused Black man with intent to lynch him, which would be illegal group action under the pretext of punishing an alleged assault, but it does not say whether he was caught or killed (A1).
Only one report was found, a Raleigh special telegram to the Richmond Dispatch (A1).
